name: Fatima Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. What you say is confidential, so tell me what you'd say publicly and what you think privately. What's a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Fatima, 43, an experienced developer at a tech company with a bachelor's degree. I maintain a reading app for children and fix its progress and answer screens; I like the moment a teacher says a child finally understood an instruction. I use AI every day for draft tests, though I still miss things and go back to the actual learner screen. My partner maintains parks, and our two school-age children can tell when I'm testing a lesson at the dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the assistant is useful for drafting little reading exercises, but someone has to see whether a child understands the instructions. I use it daily for test examples and still check them against what our learning app actually shows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If that is the extent of AI, I think my job stays solid. I have a bachelor's degree, a normal mid-level developer wage, my partner has steady work maintaining public parks, and we have about four months of expenses saved for our mortgage and two school-age children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing the reading-app progress screen and asking teachers which exercises confuse children. In the first year I'd keep using AI on made-up learner records, and transfer 120 from my pay to savings each month while both wages hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A small tool that saves time would let me fix the progress bar that keeps sticking after lesson three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did your child notice in the app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My younger child tried a practice page and thought the instruction said to tap every word. The reading app marked my child's correct answer wrong, so I sat beside them and watched where the confusion began.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would the savings transfer stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The savings transfer happens after the mortgage and school bills, not before. If either wage stops, we pause the transfer rather than let the account run below the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say coding, writing lessons and answering users are all moving targets here, so we should measure whether children learn before cutting staff. I would volunteer to test the new tools, but I would ask for a staffing plan too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the app well, but a smaller team could use AI to write both code and exercises. I might lose hours or a role, and four months saved would not last forever with a mortgage and two children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run a six-week comparison of AI-made exercise fixes and our current fixes using old, nameless learner data, counting wrong answers and teacher correction time. If the trial improves both, I'd learn the new approval workflow and ask to own a paid share of it; in the first year we'd defer a planned kitchen renovation until staffing is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with some curiosity. I want better lessons, but I also want to know who keeps getting paid to check them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which example would decide whether the trial helped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The test should include the page my child got wrong. If the AI makes the instruction shorter but leaves the same wrong mark, the score is still bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What household plan would wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I had priced the kitchen work for spring. We can wait a year rather than turn our four-month cushion into new cupboards while my job is changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 reaches our app code and exercise writing before hands-on robots appear around 2031. The children using the app still need a way to report a lesson that marks them wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my post could go quickly if one cheaper system writes and tests whole lessons. My partner's parks wage and our four-month cushion would keep the mortgage paid briefly, but there are only some other software jobs nearby, and they might be changing too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd write up the wrong-mark case and ask two nearby employers about paid accessibility-testing roles. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only to real openings whose wage with my partner's pay covers mortgage and school costs; if none qualify, I'd use savings for a wider paid-job search and ask the lender about hardship terms before missing a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can make a list, but I expect a sharp cut in the work I sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you qualified for the alternative role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Accessibility testing means checking whether a learner can use the lesson with different needs; I have done some of that in this app, but I am not a certified specialist. I'd ask what the paid job actually requires before assuming I can move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children after a cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children school stays the same while we look. I would not promise a new kitchen or a new job from an interview invitation.

I'd ask for a **learner error-report route** when automatic lessons mark answers wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years until 2031 gives firms time to show whether a person still checks how a child experiences a lesson. Robots follow around 2034, but the thinking AI changes our code first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be able to build a paid accessibility-testing role if employers still want one. My current developer post could shrink, so I would not spend on a course until a real opening or funded training path is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask an experienced tester at work to let me observe one lesson-access check each month if my manager releases the time. I'd take a specialist course only if my employer funds it and offers paid accessibility duties; in the first year after 2031 I'd apply for paid testing jobs only where vacancies exist and combined wages cover mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own post, but five years give me time to earn evidence. I can keep a wage while I test whether the other work is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check during a monthly observation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The monthly check would include my child's wrong-mark page and whether a screen reader can say the instruction clearly. I'd write down what failed before asking for a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner need to know about training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would ask if the new duties are paid and whether the course takes time away from school pickup. If either answer is vague, I would keep my present job and ask again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 gives us time to learn what children still need from a lesson when code becomes cheap. Thinking AI reaches our app in 2036; robots come around 2039 for hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might be a paid accessibility tester or still a developer. Our two wages and four-month cushion make the next few years manageable, but ten years do not guarantee a job in either field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep recording wrong-mark bugs without learner names and work with teachers to improve the screen. We'd add 120 to savings monthly while both wages hold, and in the first year after 2036 I'd move only for a signed paid testing or software offer whose combined wages cover mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years. I can learn and save without pulling our children into an imagined crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in a work record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My record would show the stuck progress bar and the wrong answer mark, with no child's name. A future employer can see how I fixed the wrong answer mark, not a copy of a child's learning history.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your older child about studying code?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older child asks whether coding is worth studying. I'd say try the subject if it is interesting, then check course costs and actual jobs when the decision comes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because both code and exercise writing could shrink before I have another paid role. A clear notice period, funded specialist training and real paid testing vacancies would help us protect the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what a wrong answer mark does to a child. My younger child thought they were bad at reading because the screen rejected a correct answer; that is a problem we owe them a fix for.

headlineQuote: My younger child thought they were bad at reading because the screen rejected a correct answer; that is a problem we owe them a fix for.
portrait: Fatima, **43**, is an experienced reading-app developer with a bachelor's degree who tests learner screens and uses AI daily.
Her **typical pay**, partner's parks wage and four-month cushion support a mortgage and two school-age children.

Steady disruption makes her **anxious** about paid hours; fast 2028 AGI alarms her about coding and lesson work.
With more time, she seeks **paid accessibility work** and funded training, then moves only for bill-covering signed offers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink both coding and exercise work before a paid testing role exists.
